content: Patients with brain tumors often experience increased intracranial pressure due to swelling of brain tissue. This swelling can make the surgical removal of brain tumors more challenging. To facilitate the surgical procedure, interventions are employed to reduce brain swelling, a process commonly referred to as brain relaxation. Brain relaxation can be achieved through the administration of intravenous fluids, such as mannitol or hypertonic saline. The purpose of this review was to compare the effects of mannitol and hypertonic saline on intraoperative brain relaxation in patients undergoing craniotomy. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to October 2013. Additional searches were conducted on specific websites, and the search was updated in January 2017, identifying five additional studies awaiting classification for future review updates. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared hypertonic saline and mannitol for brain relaxation. Studies that compared other methods of intraoperative brain relaxation with either mannitol or hypertonic saline were also included. The primary outcomes assessed were longest follow-up mortality, Glasgow Outcome Scale scores at three months, and adverse events related to the use of mannitol or hypertonic saline. Secondary outcomes included intraoperative brain relaxation, length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU), overall hospital stay, and quality of life. Standardized methods for systematic reviews, as outlined in the Cochrane Handbook, were used. Two independent reviewers extracted data on trial methodology and outcomes. Analyses were conducted on an intention-to-treat basis. A fixed-effect model was used when no significant heterogeneity was detected between studies, while a random-effects model was applied when heterogeneity was likely. The review included six RCTs with a total of 527 participants. Of these, only one trial was deemed to have a low risk of bias, while the remaining five trials were judged to have unclear or high risk of bias. None of the trials reported on the primary outcomes of longest follow-up mortality, Glasgow Outcome Scale scores at three months, or adverse events associated with mannitol or hypertonic saline. Three trials reported on secondary outcomes, including intraoperative brain relaxation, ICU stay, and hospital stay. None of the trials provided data on quality of life. In terms of brain relaxation, 42 out of 197 participants in the hypertonic saline group experienced inadequate brain relaxation, compared to 68 out of 190 participants in the mannitol group. The risk ratio for brain bulge or tense brain in the hypertonic saline group was 0.60 (95% confidence interval: 0.44 to 0.83), indicating a lower risk with hypertonic saline (low-quality evidence). One trial reported on ICU and hospital stay. The mean duration of ICU stay was 1.28 days (standard deviation: 0.5) in the mannitol group and 1.25 days (standard deviation: 0.5) in the hypertonic saline group, with no statistically significant difference (P = 0.64). The mean duration of hospital stay was 5.7 days (standard deviation: 0.7) in the mannitol group and 5.7 days (standard deviation: 0.8) in the hypertonic saline group, with no statistically significant difference (P = 1.00). Based on the limited data available, hypertonic saline appears to significantly reduce the risk of a tense brain during craniotomy compared to mannitol. However, data from a single trial suggest that ICU and hospital stays are similar between the two treatments. Further research is needed to address other important outcomes, such as long-term mortality, long-term functional outcomes, adverse events, and quality of life.
